meta.regime: Three central banks have cleared and the regime has rotated back to the oil premium: the Houthis said on October 29 they struck Ras Tanura, Rabigh and Abqaiq, and WTI is 103.010 and plus 0.99% with Brent 112.064 and plus 1.14% on TradingEconomics, undoing the one soft session Iran's conditional Hormuz offer bought. The second change is the franc, which has stopped behaving like a funding currency: USD/CHF is minus 1.04% on the month and the franc is up over 2% against the euro in October as the French ten-year nears levels last seen in 2002, so every short-franc line this file carried is cut or reversed.
meta.nextBigEvent: Governor Ueda's Bank of Japan press conference at 05:30 UTC today, the last red folder of the week and the only thing that can still reprice the yen's hawkish hold - the Bank raised FY2027 core CPI to 2.6% and lifted ETF sales to 860 billion yen, and the market has paid 0.17% for it, so a guarded Ueda hands it all back while a direct one opens December 18. Then November 3 carries both the RBA at 85-90% priced for 4.85% and the US midterms, with the Wall Street Journal reporting that Washington has warned Gulf states to prepare for a possible short, intense military campaign after that vote; the Bank of England follows on November 5 at about 94% priced for 4.00%, and the French 2027 budget goes to a vote on November 17.

dailyRead: The week's three central banks are now behind us and the board has gone back to trading the thing it was trading before them, which is oil. The Houthis said on October 29 that they had hit Ras Tanura - Saudi Arabia's largest refinery - along with Rabigh and the Aramco facility at Abqaiq, and the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted cruise missiles aimed at the west of the country. Saudi authorities have not confirmed a direct hit, there is no independently verified evidence of extensive damage, and reports say a fire near Ras Tanura was contained; the price has moved anyway. On TradingEconomics WTI is 103.010 and plus 0.99%, Brent 112.064 and plus 1.14%, and WTI is plus 10.92% on the month against plus 79.40% year to date. Wire reports put Brent nearer 115-116 and on course for a fourth consecutive monthly gain of about 14%, with WTI set for its first monthly close above 100 since April - a discrepancy named rather than smoothed, with TE the figure this file quotes. Yesterday this file wrote that Iran's conditional offer to reopen Hormuz was the first credible path to removing the premium and that the flip would be an accepted deal rather than another soft session. What arrived instead was an escalation on the other side of the Gulf, and the premium is back on after one day off. The second thing to carry out of today is a reversal in this file's own work, and it should be stated plainly rather than buried. Yesterday the franc was scored minus 1 and WEAKENING on the reasoning that the SNB had judged on September 24 that war-induced haven flows had ebbed, which made every short-franc line implicitly short a Hormuz re-escalation. That re-escalation has happened, and the franc has been going the other way for longer than one session: USD/CHF is 0.82235 and minus 0.25% on the day, minus 0.32% on the week and minus 1.04% on the month, the franc is up more than 2% against the euro in October, the Swiss ten-year has been driven down to about 0.47% by haven buying, and the French ten-year neared 4.96% on October 20 - its highest since 2002 - with the OAT-Bund spread at 156.6 basis points on October 28 after touching about 178, the widest since late 2011. The franc goes to plus 1 and MIXED, long USD/CHF is flipped to SHORT, AUD/CHF and GBP/CHF are cut from HIGH and MEDIUM to LOW-MED, and CHF/JPY comes off SHORT to RANGE. The leg that broke was the SNB's own assessment of haven demand, not the price. Third, the dollar. The data did what the hawks wanted and the dollar still did not pay: advance Q3 GDP landed at 3.4% against 3.2% forecast, September core PCE at 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y with headline PCE at 0.5% m/m and 3.6% y/y, initial claims 194K, and the composite PMI is 57.6. Against that, December Fed pricing has eased rather than firmed - CME FedWatch readings through October 29 ran from the mid-70s to about 80%, with a third-party tracker showing 84.5-88% in the morning and 77.3% by the New York close, against the 81-85% this file quoted yesterday morning - and DXY is 101.797, minus 0.07% on the day and minus 0.30% on the month, falling for a third straight session. Set that against an unemployment rate at 4.2% and rising, September payrolls at plus 29,000 and consumer confidence at 48.0, barely above its record low, and the dollar goes from plus 1 to zero: the hawkish case is intact in the data and exhausted in the price. Fourth, the Bank of Japan delivered and the yen was barely paid. The Bank held at 1.25% on an 8-1 vote with Takata Hajime dissenting for an immediate 1.5%, the Quarterly Outlook Report raised FY2027 core CPI to 2.6% from 2.4%, called price risks skewed to the upside and said underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with the price target, and the unanimous decision lifted annual ETF sales to about 860 billion yen from about 330 billion. USD/JPY is 157.440 and minus 0.17%, still plus 0.37% on the week. The yen holds plus 1 and STRENGTHENING because the policy direction is unambiguous and September unemployment fell to 2.4% from 2.5%, and it is held there rather than raised because the market has refused to pay for any of it. Ueda speaks at 05:30 UTC and is the only event left that can settle it. Fifth, the euro recovered from its own bad news. The ECB held - deposit 2.50%, main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90% - Lagarde said the hold was unanimous, that the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate and that the direction of travel is quite clear, and then she announced she will step down on 7 February 2027, nine months early, with reporting tying the timing to the April 2027 French presidential election and the wish to have a successor in place before it. EUR/USD was taken to a fresh 17-month low at 1.1105 on the statement and is now 1.11866 and plus 0.06%, which with September HICP at 3.8% from 3.2% and a December 17 hike better than 80% priced earns the euro an upgrade to plus 1 - but MIXED, not STRENGTHENING, because an open succession and a French budget vote on November 17 are both unpriced. Sixth, the policy board has compressed and that is itself the trade. Canada, Britain and Australia sit at plus 2 for three different reasons - a delivered hike into a rising oil price, a 94%-priced November 5 hike behind a cleared Budget, and the highest policy rate on the board at 4.60% with all four Australian majors now calling November 3 after CBA abandoned its pause call - while the franc, the yen and the euro sit at plus 1 and the dollar and the kiwi at zero. With no gap wider than two points anywhere on the board, the clean tickets are the two-point pairs with a dated catalyst inside a week: long GBP/USD, short USD/CAD, long GBP/NZD and short NZD/CAD. Everything at a one-point gap is a levels trade, and this file has marked it as such rather than dressing it up. Finally, the metals split. Gold is 3999.55 and minus 0.54%, which breaks the 4,000 handle this file named yesterday as its own tell for whether Hormuz risk is being priced as manageable - but it breaks it by a hundredth of a percent, with the Fed leg pushing down and the Houthi leg pulling up, so it is marked RANGE with the handle as the pivot rather than given a direction it has not earned. Silver is the cleaner read at 51.485, minus 1.26% on the day and minus 14.90% on the month, with the gold-silver ratio out to 76.8 from 75.1; copper holds at 6.5460 and plus 0.98% on the week on AI data-centre demand and a Yangshan premium at a decade high, against high US inventories and a 103-dollar crude price that works as a tax on industrial demand.

today.headline: The Bank of Japan held at 1.25% and did everything else hawkishly - 8-1 with Takata dissenting for an immediate 1.5%, FY2027 core CPI raised to 2.6% from 2.4%, price risks called skewed to the upside, underlying inflation declared to have reached the target and ETF sales lifted to about 860 billion yen a year - and USD/JPY at 157.440 and minus 0.17% has paid about a sixth of a percent for the lot
today.read: The package is unambiguous and the price response is not, and that gap is the whole yen trade right now. September unemployment fell to 2.4% from 2.5%, core CPI is 2.1% from 1.7% and the Bank has told you in its own Outlook Report that a weaker currency is part of its inflation problem - yet USD/JPY is still plus 0.37% on the week and the yen is the second-smallest mover on the board. The yen holds plus 1 and STRENGTHENING on the policy direction rather than on the tape, and JPYBASKET stays LONG by the rule at LOW-MED conviction precisely because the tape has not confirmed. Ueda speaks at 05:30 UTC and is the only thing that settles it: a guarded framing of this as patience hands the whole move back, while anything that dates December 18 opens the first real yen trend since the September hike. Tokyo core CPI at 2.6% from 2.7% is the one soft note underneath.

today.headline: The franc was the biggest mover on the board with USD/CHF at 0.82235 and minus 0.25%, and it is also the file's own reversal: scored minus 1 and WEAKENING yesterday as a funding currency, it goes to plus 1 and MIXED today
today.read: The specific leg that broke was the SNB's September 24 judgement that war-induced haven flows had ebbed, which this file used to justify every short-franc line. The flows are back and they are not one session old: USD/CHF is minus 0.32% on the week and minus 1.04% on the month, the franc is up more than 2% against the euro in October with EUR/CHF at 0.91993 and minus 0.19%, haven buying has pushed the Swiss ten-year down to about 0.47%, and the French ten-year neared 4.96% on October 20 - its highest since 2002 - with the OAT-Bund spread at 156.6 basis points on October 28 after touching about 178, the widest since late 2011. Add the Houthi strikes on Saudi refineries and the franc is long two live risk legs at once. Long USD/CHF is flipped to SHORT, AUD/CHF and GBP/CHF come off HIGH and MEDIUM to LOW-MED, and CHF/JPY comes off SHORT to RANGE. The cap on all of it is the SNB: at 0.00% with zero carry and an intervention threat it has used before, the franc gets plus 1 rather than more.

today.headline: The data was hawkish and the dollar fell for a third straight session, so the dollar goes from plus 1 to zero: advance Q3 GDP 3.4% against 3.2% forecast, September core PCE 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, headline PCE 0.5% and 3.6%, claims 194K - and December pricing eased from the 81-85% this file quoted yesterday to the mid-70s-to-80% range
today.read: This is a price call, not a data call, and the distinction is the point. On the macro the hawks are right: the composite PMI is 57.6, GDP is running 3.4% annualised, headline PCE at 3.6% is a full point and a half above target, and two governors already voted for a hike on October 28. On the price, DXY is 101.797 at minus 0.07% on the day, minus 0.01% on the week and minus 0.30% on the month, and a third-party tracker took December from 84.5-88% in the morning of October 29 to 77.3% by the New York close. The soft leg is labour and it has not improved: unemployment 4.2% and rising, September payrolls plus 29,000, job vacancies down to 7.067 million from 7.855 million, and consumer confidence at 48.0 against a record low of 44.8. A dollar that will not rally on a 3.4% GDP print with two hawkish dissents behind it is a dollar whose hawkish case is in the price. The October payroll report and the November 3 midterms are the next two tests, and the Wall Street Journal reporting that Washington has warned Gulf states to prepare for a possible short, intense campaign after that vote makes the election an oil event as well as a political one.

today.headline: Crude reversed yesterday's decline on the Houthi strikes and CAD stays plus 2: WTI 103.010 and plus 0.99%, Brent 112.064 and plus 1.14%, with USD/CAD at 1.39719 and minus 0.13% now minus 1.76% on the month - the best major performance against the dollar over that stretch
today.read: Canada is the cleanest terms-of-trade expression of the oil regime and it now has a central bank that has said so out loud. The October 28 hike to 2.50% was the first since July 2023 and Macklem called it insurance against energy pass-through, with the Monetary Policy Report lifting 2027 inflation to 3.1% from 2.0%; December is only about 42% priced, so the Bank bought optionality rather than starting a cycle, and that is the right shape for a currency whose domestic data is poor. The weak legs are real and unchanged: September employment minus 68,300, unemployment 6.5% and rising, the composite PMI 48.7 and services 48.3 both in contraction, and producer prices up 14.5% y/y, which is the pass-through Macklem is insuring against. Monthly GDP lands at 12:30 UTC today with 0.2% forecast against 0.0%. The invalidation for every CAD line in this file is the same single event - an accepted Iran deal that reopens Hormuz - and it is now a longer shot than it looked twenty-four hours ago.

today.headline: The euro took its bad news and recovered anyway: Lagarde announced she will step down on 7 February 2027, nine months early, and EUR/USD is 1.11866 and plus 0.06% after a fresh 17-month low at 1.1105 on the statement - so the euro is upgraded from zero to plus 1 and MIXED
today.read: Three things are now true at once and they do not point the same way. The hawkish leg is hard: September HICP accelerated to 3.8% from 3.2% with core at 2.5%, producer prices are up 8.2%, Lagarde said the hold was unanimous but that the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate and that the direction of travel is quite clear, and December 17 is better than 80% priced. The cooling leg is also hard: the composite PMI fell to 51.9 from 53.1, services to 51.7 from 53.0, ZEW to 18.5 from 25.8, and wage growth has slowed to 3.0% from 3.4%, which is the series that lets the Council keep waiting. The new leg is political and unpriced - an open ECB succession under the Article 283 procedure, with reporting tying the timing to the April 2027 French presidential election, on top of a French 2027 budget that goes to a vote on November 17 with Moody's at Aa3 negative since October 23. Plus 1 and MIXED is the honest resolution: own the euro on crosses against the dollar and the kiwi, not against sterling or the Canadian dollar. German preliminary October CPI at 07:29 UTC and Q3 GDP at 09:00 UTC are today's data.

today.headline: CBA abandoned its pause call and all four Australian majors now expect a hike to 4.85% on November 3 at about 85-90% priced - which is exactly why the Australian dollar is trimmed from plus 3 to plus 2, with AUD/USD at 0.70387 and plus 0.12% having gained nothing on the capitulation
today.read: The carry story is intact and the upside is gone, and those are two different statements. Australia has the highest policy rate on the board at 4.60%, headline CPI at 4.3% y/y with TE core at 3.6% and an annual trimmed mean at 3.7%, and AUD/USD is still plus 5.49% year to date, the best major of 2026. But a hike that every major and roughly nine in ten of the market now expects cannot be bought again, and the week's price action proves it: AUD/USD is plus 0.10% on the week across a CPI beat and a full round of forecast upgrades. Underneath, the domestic data is getting worse rather than better - the services PMI is 47.8 and the composite 47.7, both contracting, unemployment is at a five-year high of 4.7%, September employment fell 39,329 with full-time up 34,385 and part-time down 73,714, business confidence is minus 13 from minus 9 and consumer confidence 80.4 from 84.4. Copper at 6.5460 and plus 0.98% on the week is the one external support. Trade the score gap on AUD/NZD and AUD/CAD, not the November 3 decision; a soft labour print before Tuesday cuts the hike and the crosses together.

today.headline: The kiwi stopped falling rather than recovering - NZD/USD 0.56404 and plus 0.12%, still minus 1.01% on the week but now plus 0.65% on the month - and it is upgraded from minus 1 to zero and MIXED on the stabilisation plus a sharp turn up in the domestic surveys
today.read: This is a deliberate refusal to keep selling a two-day-old decision. The October 28 hold at 2.75% on a 4-3 vote against a 3.00% consensus was a genuine shock to pricing, but the Bank's own September track had already pointed to an October pause and a December hike, which makes it market mispricing rather than an RBNZ pivot - and Breman said rates may even be higher than the September meeting implied and flagged concern that a sustained weak kiwi adds to imported inflation. The domestic data has turned: the manufacturing PMI is 56.5 from 53.3, consumer confidence 89.5 from 80.4, business confidence 52.5 from 51.9, the composite 53.4, and Q2 annual GDP 2.6% from 1.7%. Against that, Q3 CPI eased to 3.7% from 4.1%, unemployment is 5.6% and rising, and at 2.75% this is the second-lowest rate on the board. Zero and MIXED, with the biases moved to RANGE against the dollar while the two-point gaps against sterling and the Canadian dollar stay short. December 9 carries a full Monetary Policy Statement at TE's 3.00% forecast; the general election is November 7.

today.headline: Sterling did nothing and did not need to - GBP/USD 1.33861 and plus 0.07%, plus 0.06% on the week and plus 1.44% on the month - holding the level it took after the Budget cleared, with November 5 about 94% priced for 4.00%
today.read: The pound is the file's best-supported major on policy and the quietest currency on the board, which is the combination worth owning. The tail is behind it: the October 28 Budget passed with ten-year gilts 2.1 basis points lower and the thirty-year 4.5 lower, and the OBR put headroom at 15 billion pounds against 24 billion forecast in March - at the low end of the pre-Budget cluster but inside it. In front of it is a dated catalyst with a near-certain outcome and an undecided path: a market-implied tracker put November 5 at about 94% on October 28, a Reuters poll had 54 of 63 economists at 25 basis points to 4.00%, and the September vote was 6-3 to hold, so the vote split and the Monetary Policy Report are what actually trade on the day. September CPI at 3.5% from 3.1% with core at 2.8% is the mandate, and the surveys have turned up - services PMI 53.1 from 52.1, manufacturing 52.8 from 51.9, composite 53.1 from 52.0. The soft legs to watch are the claimant count at plus 30,300 from plus 7,000 and consumer confidence at minus 24 from minus 13. Long GBP/USD and long GBP/NZD are the two cleanest two-point tickets on the board.

The October 29 data supported them without moving pricing in their favour: advance Q3 GDP 3.4%, core PCE 0.3% m/m and 3.1% y/y, headline PCE 0.5% and 3.6%, claims 194K. EUR.when: December 17, one of Lagarde's last meetings
EUR.note: Held on October 29 - deposit 2.50%, main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90% - and the press conference firmed December rather than the statement: Lagarde said the hold was unanimous, that the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate, that the direction of travel is quite clear on rates and that the inter-meeting period gives the Council a lot more information. September HICP at 3.8% from 3.2% with core at 2.5% is the case. The new fact is institutional: she steps down on 7 February 2027, so December 17 is one of her last meetings and the succession is open under the Article 283 procedure.

GBP.note: Bank Rate is 3.75% and TradingEconomics carries a 4.0% forecast for November 5. A market-implied tracker put the hike at about 94% on October 28 and a Reuters poll had 54 of 63 economists calling 25 basis points to 4.00%, with views split on what follows. September CPI at 3.5% from 3.1% with core at 2.8% is the driver, the September vote was 6-3 to hold, and the Budget passed on October 28 without a gilt accident, which removed the one tail that could have stopped it. The Monetary Policy Report and vote split carry the path beyond November.

JPY.note: Held at 1.25% on October 30 on an 8-1 vote, with Takata dissenting for an immediate 1.5% on the argument that underlying inflation has reached the target. The Quarterly Outlook Report raised FY2027 core CPI to 2.6% from 2.4%, called price risks skewed to the upside and named yen depreciation among the drivers, and the Bank unanimously lifted annual ETF sales to about 860 billion yen from about 330 billion from January 2027. AUD.note: Cash rate 4.60%, the highest on this board, and TradingEconomics forecasts 4.85% for November 3. Pricing sits at about 85-90% after the September-quarter CPI - Bloomberg data cited at about 85%, CBA near 90%, StoneX above 80% - and all four majors now call the hike after CBA abandoned its pause and reframed it as an insurance hike, which is the change since yesterday. Headline CPI 4.3% y/y with TE core at 3.6% and the annual trimmed mean at 3.7%. Market pricing now puts the peak near 5% around mid-2027.

NZD.when: December 9, with a full Monetary Policy Statement
NZD.note: Held the OCR at 2.75% on October 28 on a 4-3 vote against a 3.00% consensus, and TradingEconomics forecasts 3.00% for December 9. The framing matters more than the surprise: the Bank's own September track had already pointed to an October pause and a December hike, so the dovish shock was market mispricing rather than an RBNZ pivot, and Governor Breman said rates may even be higher than the September meeting implied while flagging concern that a sustained weak kiwi adds to imported inflation. Q3 CPI 3.7% from 4.1%, core 3.2%. The general election falls on November 7.

CAD.note: Raised the overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.50% on October 28, the first increase since July 2023, and TradingEconomics carries 2.50% as its December 9 forecast. Macklem framed it as insurance against energy pass-through - needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill into the rest of the economy - while refusing a sequence: no predetermined path, one meeting at a time, further increases proceeding carefully. December is about 42% priced, so this is optionality bought rather than a cycle started. The Monetary Policy Report lifted 2027 inflation to 3.1% from 2.0% and 2026 growth to 1.0% from 0.7%.

CHF.note: The policy rate is 0.00% and TradingEconomics shows no move expected on December 10. The SNB's lever is intervention rather than the rate, and that lever has come back into play: minutes attributed the inflation uptick to higher oil prices and franc depreciation, and the Bank judged on September 24 that its threat to sell francs was no longer needed because war-induced haven flows had ebbed. The franc is now up over 2% against the euro in October with EUR/CHF at 0.91993, which puts it back near the area the Bank previously threatened to defend. September CPI 1.0% from 0.8%, core 0.5%.

catalysts.note: Released. The Bank held the OCR at 2.75% against a 3.00% forecast and pricing near 90%, on a 4-3 vote. catalysts.event: New Zealand: RBNZ press conference with Governor Breman (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held. Breman said further increases are likely at coming meetings, that rates may even be higher than the September meeting implied, and that the Committee is concerned a sustained weak New Zealand dollar adds to imported inflation. Read alongside the September track, that makes December 9 - which carries a full Monetary Policy Statement, with TE forecasting 3.00% - the live meeting rather than a formality.

catalysts.event: United Kingdom: Annual Budget Release (HM Treasury red folder)
catalysts.note: Delivered, and the tail did not happen. Ten-year gilt yields fell 2.1 basis points to 5.321% on Tradeweb and the thirty-year 4.5 basis points to around 5.70%, sterling was largely unmoved and the FTSE All-Share flat. catalysts.note: Delivered. The overnight rate rose 25 basis points to 2.50%, in line with consensus and the first increase since July 2023, and TradingEconomics carries the new rate. The Monetary Policy Report carried the content rather than the decision: 2027 inflation to 3.1% from the 2.0% projected in July and 2026 growth to 1.0% from 0.7%. The Houthi strikes on Saudi oil infrastructure have since validated the energy-pass-through framing.

catalysts.event: Canada: Bank of Canada press conference with Governor Macklem (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held. Macklem framed the hike as insurance against energy pass-through - needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill into the rest of the economy - while refusing a sequence: no predetermined path, decisions one meeting at a time, further increases proceeding carefully. December 9 is about 42% priced and TE forecasts 2.50%, so this is optionality bought rather than a cycle started.

catalysts.event: United States: Federal Funds Rate decision and FOMC Statement (red folder)
catalysts.note: Released. The target range was held at 3-3/4 to 4 percent and the statement was approved 10-2, with Lisa D. Cook and Beth M. Hammack voting against because they preferred to raise the range by a quarter point. Hammack dissented the same way in July; for Cook it is the first dissent of her four years in the post. The statement says inflation remains elevated, that job gains have kept pace with the workforce and that the unemployment rate has changed little, and it does not mention energy prices.

catalysts.event: United States: FOMC press conference with Chair Warsh (red folder)
catalysts.note: Held. The energy channel in this file's read came from the podium rather than from the Committee's text, which does not mention energy prices at all. Two days and one GDP print later, the market's verdict is that the hawkish case is in the price: December pricing has eased to the mid-70s-to-80% range from the 81-85% quoted yesterday morning, and DXY has fallen three sessions in a row to 101.797.

Advance Q3 GDP printed above forecast at 3.4% against 3.2% expected and 2.2% previously, and September core PCE landed in line at 0.3% m/m with the annual rate at 3.1%; headline PCE rose 0.5% m/m to 3.6% y/y. catalysts.note: Released. All three rates held as forecast - deposit facility 2.50%, main refinancing 2.65%, marginal lending 2.90% - and TradingEconomics carries the unchanged levels. The statement alone drove EUR/USD to a fresh 17-month low at 1.1105; the pair has since recovered to 1.11866.

catalysts.note: Held, and it reversed the statement's move. Lagarde said the hold was decided unanimously, that the Governing Council debated whether a hike was appropriate, that the direction of travel is quite clear on rates and that the inter-meeting period gives the Council a lot more information; she stayed non-committal on activating the Transmission Protection Instrument, saying only that the ECB has instruments to respond should market developments threaten transmission. December 17 is better than 80% priced.

catalysts.event: Euro area: ECB President Lagarde announces she will step down on 7 February 2027
catalysts.note: Confirmed by the ECB's own press release: Lagarde informed the Governing Council and European Council President Antonio Costa that she will step down on 7 February 2027, nine months before her term ends, and the release gives no reason. The successor is appointed under Article 283 of the TFEU following a Council recommendation and consultation with the European Parliament and the Governing Council. Reporting ties the timing to the April 2027 French presidential election and the wish to settle the appointment before it. December 17 is one of her last meetings.

catalysts.note: Released. The Bank held the policy rate at 1.25% as forecast, on an 8-1 vote with Takata Hajime dissenting for an immediate 1.5% on the argument that underlying consumer inflation has reached the 2% target. The statement said underlying inflation has reached levels consistent with the price target, and the Bank unanimously raised annual ETF sales to about 860 billion yen from about 330 billion from January 2027. USD/JPY is 157.440 and minus 0.17%.

catalysts.note: Released, and it carried more than the decision. FY2027 core CPI was raised to 2.6% from 2.4% and core-core to 2.7%, FY2028 core-core was kept at 2.3%, price risks were called skewed to the upside with an explicit risk of underlying inflation deviating above 2 percent, and yen depreciation was named among the drivers with foreign exchange in the risk list. catalysts.event: Japan: BoJ press conference with Governor Ueda (red folder)
catalysts.note: Not yet held at the time of writing - it begins at 05:30 UTC and is the last red folder of the week. It is the only event that can still reprice the yen's hawkish hold: the market has paid 0.17% for an 8-1 vote, an upgraded FY2027 inflation path and a near-tripling of ETF sales, so a guarded framing of all this as patience hands the move back, while anything that dates December 18 opens the first real yen trend since the September hike.

catalysts.note: Eased to 2.6% from 2.7% - the one soft note under the Bank of Japan's hawkish package, and the data point that argues against its own upgraded FY2027 path. September national unemployment fell to 2.4% from 2.5% in the same release window.

catalysts.note: Ten days after a 4-3 hold and two days after the Bank of England, this is the unpriced two-sided tail under every kiwi line in this file. catalysts.note: Better than 80% priced for a hike after Lagarde said the Governing Council debated whether one was appropriate and that the direction of travel is quite clear. The next ECB wage tracker, against wage growth already slowing to 3.0% from 3.4%, is the series that could let the Council wait again.

catalysts.event: Strait of Hormuz, Saudi oil infrastructure and the insurance premium
catalysts.note: The premium is priced off insurable risk rather than off volumes: war-risk cover is quoted at 6-10% of hull value per transit against 0.15-0.25% before the war, the IMO said on October 27 that the route contains mines and that it cannot guarantee safe transit, and transits fell from 85 a day to four by October 18. Iran's October 28 offer to reopen the strait within four to five days if the United States lifts its blockade remains the single event that deflates the premium, and the Houthi strikes of October 29 are the reason it has not.

geopolitics: The transmission chain is unchanged and what changed is the direction of travel along it. Yesterday this file wrote that Iran's conditional offer to reopen Hormuz within four to five days if the United States lifted its blockade was the first credible path to removing the crude premium, and that the flip would be an accepted deal rather than another soft session. What arrived instead was an escalation on the other side of the Gulf: the Houthis said on October 29 they had struck Ras Tanura - Saudi Arabia's largest refinery - along with Rabigh and Aramco's facility at Abqaiq, and the Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted cruise missiles fired toward the west of the country. Saudi authorities have not confirmed a direct hit, there is no independently verified evidence of extensive damage and a fire near Ras Tanura was reported contained, so part of the move is premium rather than barrels - but the premium is what trades. On TradingEconomics WTI is 103.010 and plus 0.99%, Brent 112.064 and plus 1.14%, with WTI plus 10.92% on the month and plus 79.40% year to date; wire reports put Brent nearer 115-116 and on course for a fourth consecutive monthly gain of about 14%, with WTI set for its first monthly close above 100 since April, and that divergence is named rather than smoothed, with TE the figure this file quotes. The physical facts underneath have not changed: the IRGC declared the strait closed on October 26, the International Maritime Organization said on October 27 that the Hormuz route contains mines and that it cannot guarantee safe transit, more than thirty very large crude carriers have been damaged with eleven hit in October alone, war-risk cover is quoted at 6-10% of hull value per transit against 0.15-0.25% before the war, and transits fell from 85 a day to four by October 18. CENTCOM disputes the closure. The new escalation vector is political and dated: the Wall Street Journal reports that Washington has warned several Gulf Arab states to prepare for the possibility of a short, intense military campaign after the November 3 US election, and ExxonMobil and Chevron have cancelled executive travel to the UAE's largest oil show next week - which puts the US midterms on the oil calendar and is why USOIL is upgraded to MEDIUM conviction. The FX read has one genuine reversal in it today. Crude is the terms-of-trade leg under a plus 2 Canada, so the Bank of Canada's October 28 hike to 2.50% - explicitly insurance against energy pass-through, with 2027 inflation lifted to 3.1% from 2.0% - has been validated rather than undercut, and short USD/CAD, short NZD/CAD, short EUR/CAD, long CAD/JPY and long CAD/CHF all still share one invalidation: an accepted Iran deal. The franc is where this file was wrong. It was scored minus 1 and WEAKENING yesterday on the SNB's September 24 judgement that war-induced haven flows had ebbed, which made every short-franc line implicitly short a Hormuz re-escalation; that re-escalation has happened and the flows were already returning. USD/CHF is minus 1.04% on the month, the franc is up over 2% against the euro in October, haven buying has pushed the Swiss ten-year down to about 0.47%, and the French ten-year neared 4.96% on October 20 - its highest since 2002. So long USD/CHF is flipped to SHORT, AUD/CHF and GBP/CHF are cut from HIGH and MEDIUM to LOW-MED, CAD/CHF is cut to LOW-MED as a position that is now long the oil premium and short the haven premium simultaneously, EUR/CHF comes off long to RANGE and CHF/JPY off short to RANGE. The cap on all of it is the SNB: at 0.00% with EUR/CHF at 0.91993 the franc is back near the area the Bank previously threatened to defend with franc sales, and December 10 is the date it can say so. Japan is the most energy-import-levered economy here and its own Outlook Report named higher oil and yen depreciation among the inflation drivers it has just upgraded, which makes the BoJ a second-order Hormuz trade in both directions and Ueda at 05:30 UTC the week's last binary. Gold at 3999.55 has lost the 4,000 handle this file named as its own tell, but by a hundredth of a percent, with the Fed leg pushing down and the Houthi leg pulling up - so it is marked RANGE with the handle as the pivot. The European political risk sits apart from all of this and is the reason EU50 is scored on its own evidence: the French 2027 budget goes to a vote on November 17 against a 5.0% deficit target with no majority behind it, Moody's held Aa3 with a negative outlook on October 23, the OAT-Bund spread is 156.6 basis points after touching about 178 - the widest since late 2011 - FR40 is minus 2.30% on the year while DE40 is plus 8.58%, and Euro Stoxx Banks is minus 9.76% on the month. Lagarde's announcement that she leaves on 7 February 2027, with reporting tying the timing to the April 2027 French presidential election, layers an open ECB succession on top of it. Three political dates sit inside the next three weeks: the US midterms on November 3, the New Zealand general election on November 7 and the French budget vote on November 17.
